First, look at your ban screen. If it says "Decision method: We used automated systems" and "More details aren't available," screenshot it. That proves a bot banned you with zero evidence and no human review.

Second, the standard support form is useless right now. Email privacy@roblox.com with the subject "GDPR Article 15 Data Access Request." Tell them you want all your chat logs and moderation records. If the bot replies telling you to use the self-serve portal, reply back and say "I cannot use self-serve because my account is banned. Please assist me via this ticket." That forces their legal team to open a real ticket for you.

Third, if they claim they can't verify your email or you get a weird login error, check your Google Play or Apple receipts. Send them the order number. Billing proof is undeniable and proves you own the account.

Fourth, if you want to try the fast unban that worked for some people, submit a ticket saying you apologize for the misunderstanding, you understand the automated system is sensitive even in Trusted DMs, and you'll be more careful. It sucks to apologize for a bot's mistake, but it works for some.

Fifth, if you're in the EU, use your rights. File a free dispute with ADR Center under Article 21 of the DSA. File with Verbraucherzentrale if you're in Germany. text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

text:
An extract from an article by Avay Shukla relevent to today's judgement on Swatantra  Bhardwaj bail-
'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.
The Tribune 19 July 2026

CENTRE TELLS SC AHMEDABAD CRASH PROBE NEARLY DONE

The Centre told the Supreme Court on Wednesday that its probe into the June 12, 2025 Air India crash in Ahmedabad has entered its closing stage. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta sought a two to three week adjournment, saying investigators must finish work under international procedures.

The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau had earlier been expected to place its draft final report before the court in early October, in a sealed cover. Petitioners, including the father of the deceased pilot and the Safety Matters Foundation, want an independent, court supervised probe and public release of the final report.

The AAIB said cockpit voice and airborne image recordings cannot be shared with an outside committee or the public under the Aircraft (Investigation of Accidents and Incidents) Rules, 2025. Flight AI-171, a Boeing 787-8 headed to London Gatwick, crashed soon after leaving Ahmedabad. It killed 260 people, including former Gujarat chief minister Vijay Rupani.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Supreme Court stays GST demands on corporate guarantees: what the interim order does, and what it leaves untouched

The Supreme Court has stayed the GST demands raised on corporate guarantees given within groups, pending a challenge to the Gujarat High Court's August 2026 ruling on Rule 28(2) of the CGST Rules. The stay is interim. It does not decide taxability and it does not strike down the rule.

For groups sitting on show cause notices or adjudication orders on guarantees given to banks for subsidiaries, this buys time. It does not buy certainty.

Background

Rule 28(2) was inserted by Notification 52/2023-Central Tax with effect from 26 October 2023. It values a corporate guarantee given to a related person at 1% per annum of the amount guaranteed, or the actual consideration, whichever is higher. Circular 204/16/2023-GST of 27 October 2023 explained the rule, and Circular 225/19/2024-GST of 11 July 2024 answered a list of trade questions. Notification 12/2024-Central Tax then amended the rule retrospectively from 26 October 2023 to extend the benefit of the second proviso to Rule 28(1): where the recipient is eligible for full ITC, the invoice value is deemed to be the value of supply.

Circular 225 also settled the mechanics. Guarantees issued or renewed before 26 October 2023 are valued under the old Rule 28; those issued or renewed on or after that date fall under Rule 28(2). Value is based on the amount guaranteed, not the amount disbursed. A multi-year guarantee is taxed at issuance at 1% for each year of its term, pro-rated for part years, and each renewal is a fresh supply. Co-guarantors share the value in proportion to the amount each guarantees. A foreign related party guaranteeing an Indian entity's borrowing triggers reverse charge in India, and Rule 28(2) does not apply where the recipient is outside India.

The Gujarat High Court ruling

On 14 August 2026, a Division Bench of the Gujarat High Court partly allowed a batch of petitions. It upheld Rule 28(2) and section 15(4) of the CGST Act, and accepted that a guarantee given to a related person without consideration is a taxable supply. It read down the words "whichever is higher" as arbitrary, because they deny the guarantor the option of using the actual charge. In the matters before it, actual charges ranged between 0.25% and 0.3%, well below the 1% deemed value.

The High Court also held the 1% valuation harsh for guarantees given before 26 October 2023, while keeping liability from that date. It quashed section 74 proceedings where there was no deliberate suppression; one notice of August 2024 related to a guarantee of February 2012. It directed refund of excess GST, set aside the conflicting circular clarifications and allowed three months for implementation.

What the Supreme Court has done

Petitions against that judgment came up on 16 November 2026 before a Bench of Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice Vipul M. Pancholi. The Court issued notice, returnable in four weeks, and stayed the impugned demands until further orders. The order records no findings on merits.

Read it narrowly. The demands in the matters before the Court are stayed. Rule 28(2) stands. The Gujarat reading-down stands as one High Court's view, now under challenge. Officers elsewhere may continue to issue notices, and other High Courts are not bound by the Gujarat ruling.

Who is affected

Indian holding companies that guarantee bank loans of subsidiaries, step-down entities and joint ventures. Promoter-group entities that cross-guarantee each other's working capital limits. Indian subsidiaries of foreign groups where the parent guarantees local borrowings, since they pay under reverse charge. Lenders and statutory auditors who need to know whether the guarantor's books carry a contingent GST exposure.

The practitioner's view

The real money in these disputes is rarely the tax on fully creditable transactions. Where the borrowing subsidiary is a regular taxpayer entitled to full ITC, the second proviso to Rule 28(1) lets the invoice value stand, and whatever the parent pays comes back to the group as credit. The exposure sits in three places: recipients making exempt supplies or otherwise not eligible for full credit, pre-October 2023 periods where notices have applied the 1% yardstick, and section 74 notices that use the extended period to reach back several years.

The stay helps the petitioners directly. For everyone else it signals that the Supreme Court sees a serious question. That is a reason to defend notices on merits and limitation, not a reason to ignore them. An order left unappealed within time becomes final, whatever the Supreme Court later decides.

The second issue is records. Many groups do not keep a register of guarantees with amount, tenure, renewal dates and the borrower's ITC position. Without it, exposure cannot be computed under either reading of the rule.

Take an illustration on the circular's method. A parent guarantees a ₹100 crore term loan of its subsidiary for five years. Value is 5% of ₹100 crore, that is ₹5 crore, taxed at issuance at 18%, giving ₹90 lakh. If the subsidiary is entitled to full ITC, the invoice value can be accepted under the second proviso and the tax is a timing cost. If the subsidiary's outward supplies are partly exempt, that relief is not available and part of the ₹90 lakh becomes a real cost. Under the Gujarat reading, an actual charge of 0.3% a year would give a value of ₹1.5 crore instead.

Action points

1. Build a guarantee register for every guarantee issued or renewed since July 2017: beneficiary, lender, amount, term, renewals, fee charged and the borrower's ITC eligibility.

2. Split the exposure into periods before and after 26 October 2023, since the valuation rule and the litigation position differ.

3. Where a notice invokes section 74, test it for actual suppression. Disclosure in audited financial statements and in the borrower's records weakens any allegation of intent.

4. File replies and appeals within time, and ask that proceedings be kept in abeyance by citing the pending Supreme Court matter. Do not let an order become final by default.

5. For new guarantees, document the fee on arm's length lines and the borrower's eligibility for full ITC, so the second proviso to Rule 28(1) can be applied cleanly.

6. Where the guarantor is abroad, confirm that the Indian borrower is paying under reverse charge and taking the matching credit.

7. Brief the statutory auditor on the contingent liability and the basis for any provision or disclosure.

The stay gives four weeks of breathing room and, in practice, probably far more. Use it to put the facts in order, because when the Court rules, the group with clean records will be better placed whichever way it goes.

This is general information, not advice on any specific case.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

The Bombay High Court on Friday struck down the amendments to Information Technology (IT) Rules allowing the Central government to establish Fact-Check Units. 

Comedian Kunal Kamra has filed a petition against the Centre's move to establish Fact-Check Units to identify and debunk 'fake and misleading' information about its functioning on social media platforms under the Press Information Bureau (PIB). 

Under the new rules, if the fact check unit comes across or is informed about any posts that are “fake”, “false” or contain “misleading” facts pertaining to the business of the government, it would flag it to the social media intermediaries.

The online intermediaries would then have to take down such content if they wanted to retain their “safe harbour” (legal immunity against third-party content).

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Good morning, happy Sunday, and welcome to the weekly update. This week's topics:

1. My Two Cents: False Alarms at the Maritime Centre
2. Floating Dock for Fire Boat 1
3. New Rescue Boat
4. Electric Vehicles
5. HRFE is Hiring: EVT

---
1. Common false alarms are something HRFE, and I assume many other fire departments, deal with. Smoke from Brothers Meats on Agricola, the crematorium on King, or flames from the Bedford Sewage plant are all common false alarms for HRFE. A report of "smoke", which is actually steam, coming from a mechanical room on the middle floors of the Maritime Centre is one of HRFE's most prominent false alarms. Here's my two cents on the issue.

I think it is time that they take a look at how these calls are getting dispatched. Every time this call comes in, it gets paged out as a full first alarm structure fire assignment, which means three engines, an aerial, a chief, a tactical unit, and a platoon captain. All units going code one, lights and sirens.

At a certain point, in my opinion, given the very specific and predictable fact pattern, the risk of this being a fire does not dictate sending seven units code one to this call. Yes, I understand, everything is treated as a fire until proven otherwise. However, there's a reason backup units go code three to fire alarms activated. The risk, in my view, doesn't dictate all units starting out code one. I would argue a single caller ten blocks away reporting they can see white steam from the mechanical room for the sixth time in a couple months is a condition that warrants HRFE adjusting the response in some manner.

Another item that has been raised is fines. My understanding is that generally the building is not being issued an Alarm Systems Notification (ASN) for these types of calls, so I highly doubt the building is being fined. I'm OK with that - it isn't the Maritime Centre's fault if someone calls this condition in from ten blocks away.  That's not really what ASNs are for. In terms of other remedies, I don't know what jurisdiction the department would have to ask or order the building to make some type of change to the steam production. I doubt HRFE has much authority to order that. So, given that  I don't think they can force the building into anything, and given that they can't stop people from calling this in, I think the department needs to take a close look at adjusting responses to this particular fact pattern to align with the potential risk.

I don't have a strong opinion about what the response should be, but seven units going code one to these calls seems quite frankly ridiculous. My own view is it should probably be a single-unit response for an investigation call, unless the information from the caller differs from the typical fact pattern. However, my main point is they need to review this response and not keep simply sending a full first alarm no matter how predictable the outcome is. This same false alarm with the exact same fact pattern has come in at least two dozen times in the last couple of years, needlessly tying up resources that could be available for other calls.

Some may not agree with this, and I can already hear people saying "well there's no way they'll adjust the response because what if that one time, it is a fire". Well, to be honest, I think this is an invalid argument. First off, by that logic, why not send a full first alarm to every automatic alarm? There's a reason one unit goes code one and the rest go code three on an automatic alarm. There's a reason one unit gets assigned for a generic "smoke in the area" type calls, etc. Those responses are generated proportionate to the risk. Secondly, every one of these Maritime Centre calls is coming in with a very specific fact pattern: one caller, far away from the building, "smoke" around the 10th floor, etc. If the fact pattern comes in differently, of course sending a full first alarm might make sense. However,  sending a full first alarm response with everybody going code one is not a proportionate response to that one same predictable fact pattern, in my opinion. Check it out? Absolutely. Seven units code one? I cannot follow that logic.

Feel free to disagree, but since people have asked, there's my two cents on the Maritime Centre.

---
2. HRM has issued a tender for a floating dock for Fire Boat 1. It sounds like this is going to be installed in the same or a similar position to where the Fire Boat is docked currently, at Alderney Marina. The tender calls for a floating dock setup with lighting and a power connection, I believe for the boat. Having discussed it with a couple of people, it sounds like this is something crews were hoping for and that it will improve FB01 operations. Good to see

---
3. HRM has also issued a tender for a new rescue boat. There isn't a ton of detail in the tender documents. It states they're looking for a 16' polyethylene boat for rescue purposes. It doesn't even say explicitly it is for HRFE, although I think that is a fairly safe assumption given it is for rescue purposes. I stand to be corrected but I think 16' would make it slightly larger than most of the Zodiac boats currently in the field (Rescue Boats 6, 9, 14, 23, 26, 38, 42, 45). Given the specs they have listed, I'm fairly confident this is a lake boat, not a harbour boat, and also there's no indication it will have any firefighting capacity. Will share more details when I get them.

---
4. The province of NS has developed an electric vehicle registry. The fire department has an obvious interest in electric vehicles given that they present different challenges than traditional vehicles. Here are some statistics from the registry:

5. HRFE is hiring a mechanic, also known as an EVT (Emergency Vehicle Technician). You can see the job posting here: https://t.co/YKRSrToWD9

🔸The Challenge to the DPDP Act
- Petitioner
DNPA (21 publishers); petition filed 6 October, stay sought 27 October.

- Concerns
Could expose sources, force removal of reports and deter whistleblowers.

- Consent problem
Seeking consent from subjects = 'pre-censorship' (Madhavi Divan).

- No exemption
The Act has no specific journalistic exemption.

🔸Relevant Provisions of the DPDP Act
- Section 3(c)(ii)
Excludes data made public by the person or under a legal duty – a limited exclusion.

- Sections 4–6
Grounds, notice and consent for processing personal data.

- Section 8
Duties of data fiduciaries – security, accuracy, erasure.

- Section 17
Exemptions for legal proceedings, law enforcement, research – not journalism.

🔸The Constitutional Balance
- Right to Privacy
Article 21 – dignity, autonomy, personal data (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017).

- Press freedom
Article 19(1)(a) – investigate and report on public interest.

- Limits
Both are not absolute; Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions.

🔸Key Judgments
- R. Rajagopal (1994)
'Auto Shankar case' – officials can't use privacy to block reports on official conduct; no prior restraint.

- R.K. Anand (2009)
Upheld a sting operation exposing an attempt to subvert the BMW trial.

- Manu Sharma (2010)
Warned against media trials that turn suspects into convicts.

- Sahara v. SEBI (2012)
Courts may postpone reporting if there is real risk to a fair trial.

- Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014)
Sting journalism gives no blanket immunity for unlawful acts.

- Axel Springer v. Germany (2012)
ECHR Grand Chamber (12–5) upheld a newspaper's report on an actor's arrest as public-interest journalism.

🔸Global Approaches
- USA
First Amendment; Privacy Protection Act, 1980 limits searches of journalists' work.

- UK
Data Protection Act, 2018 – exemption if publication is in the public interest.

- Brazil
General Data Protection Law excludes journalisticprocessing.

- Kenya
Section 52, Data Protection Act, 2019 – conditional exemption.

- International law
Articles 17 & 19 ICCPR; Articles 8 & 10 ECHR.

🔸Way Forward
- Journalistic exemption
A narrow, public-interest exemption in the DPDP framework.

- Public interest test
Separate genuine scrutiny from needless intrusion.

- Source protection
Protect sources while ensuring accuracy and fairness.

- Proportionality
Restrictions must be necessary and proportionate.

Deep Concern over the Removal of Millions of Muslim Names from India's Revised Electoral Rolls

Bangladesh Islami Chhatrashibir has expressed deep concern over the removal of nearly 130 million names from India's nationwide electoral rolls through the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process, warning that the voting rights and citizenship security of a significant number of eligible Muslim voters could be jeopardised. Central President Nurul Islam and Secretary General Sibgatullah voiced this concern in a joint statement issued today, 16 November (Monday).

In the statement, the leaders noted: "According to reports published by various international and local media outlets, the proportion of Muslims among those excluded from India's nationwide electoral roll revision process is disproportionately high. In West Bengal alone, approximately 2.7 million voters have been excluded following the adjudication process under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), nearly 70 per cent of whom are Muslims. Despite possessing valid identity documents and family records, many Bengali-speaking Muslims have had their names removed from the electoral rolls. There have also been allegations that, in the course of this process, many of them are being detained on accusations of being 'illegal infiltrators' and forcibly expelled into Bangladesh. Such actions constitute clear violations of international human rights conventions."

Referring to India's existing electoral and constitutional framework, the leaders emphasised: "Under Section 21(3) of India's Representation of the People Act, 1950, the Election Commission of India (ECI) is empowered to direct a special revision of electoral rolls. However, Section 22 of the same Act and Rule 21A of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, require proper verification of information, a reasonable opportunity for the individuals concerned to present their cases, and decisions in accordance with established legal procedures before any name is removed from the electoral rolls. Furthermore, Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India guarantee equality before the law and prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, respectively. Therefore, curtailing any citizen's voting rights or subjecting them to discriminatory treatment on the basis of religious identity runs contrary to the constitutional principles of the country."

The statement also highlighted the broader pattern of discrimination against Muslims in India, with the leaders observing: "The process of restricting the civil and fundamental rights of Muslims in India is not an isolated incident; rather, it is part of a long-term state and legal agenda. The controversial Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and the National Register of Citizens (NRC) have facilitated the development of a discriminatory framework for determining citizenship on the basis of religious identity. In addition, measures and actions such as the abrogation of Article 370, the law on triple talaq, attempts to impose a Uniform Civil Code (UCC), the Waqf property amendment law, restrictions imposed by various states on cow slaughter and beef consumption, the demolition of mosques, and the demolition of Muslim homes and other structures using bulldozers have undermined the religious, social, and economic rights of Muslims. The current electoral roll revision process is a clear manifestation of this continuing pattern of discriminatory measures, reflecting a policy of 'identify, exclude and expel.'"

Emphasising the fundamental responsibility of the state to protect the rights of its citizens, the leaders declared: "Ensuring citizens' voting rights and security is one of the primary responsibilities of any state. Depriving any community of its voting rights or subjecting its members to harassment over questions of citizenship on the basis of their religious identity is wholly unacceptable.

We strongly urge the Government of the Republic of India to immediately halt the discriminatory removal of names from the electoral rolls, reinstate the names of genuine and eligible voters, and cease unlawful detentions and the forcible expulsion of individuals into Bangladesh."

The leaders also called upon the international community to abandon double standards in the application of human rights principles. They urged the United Nations, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), and international human rights organisations to take effective measures to safeguard the fundamental human rights and civil rights of Muslims belonging to India's minority community.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

"Whoever films, I'll break their mother's bones": Teen beaten by inspectors, but case closed | Documentation

A 17-year-old who boarded a bus in Jerusalem without a Rav-Kav transit card confronted four inspectors who attacked him and threatened other passengers. Although part of the incident was captured on video, the police closed the case, explaining: "The conduct of all involved parties was taken into consideration." The complainant has filed an appeal.

Gilad Cohen | Published: 11.17.26 

The police have closed an investigation file against four bus inspectors who were filmed about a year and a half ago beating a 17-year-old who confronted them on Egged bus line 39A in Jerusalem. In footage obtained by ynet, one of the inspectors is seen threatening passengers who filmed the incident: 

"Whoever films—I'll break their mother's bones. Take out your phone and delete the videos right now." The teenager filed an appeal against the decision to close the case, and police stated that the matter is under review by the State Attorney’s Appeals Department.

The incident took place on the evening of March 10, 2025. The complainant boarded an Egged bus on Herzl Boulevard in Jerusalem and stated he only realized then that he did not have his Rav-Kav card with him. A few stops later, the four inspectors boarded and began checking passengers. When they reached the teenager and he stated he had no card, a confrontation broke out during which he was struck.

In the footage, one of the inspectors can be heard shouting at him, "Sit down quietly, why did you touch me?", to which the teen replies, "I didn't touch you." At one point, the inspector yells, "I'll f*** your mother." The teen says, "I'm sorry... I'm deleting everything, don't hit me."
According to the appeal, filed via attorney Haim Bleicher from the Honenu organization, the inspectors forcibly took a camera from one of the female passengers, deleted the footage, and forced her and the other passengers off the bus while cursing at them. They instructed the driver to continue driving. 

From that moment on, it is claimed, the teenager was left alone with the inspectors, who beat him in the face and body and deleted the videos he had recorded on his mobile phone.

The teenager claims that the first part of the assault was recorded on the inspectors' body cameras, but at a certain point, they turned them off, and three of them continued to beat him for long minutes. One of them, it is claimed, tore his wallet, pulled out his identity card, and issued him a fine. According to him, they put him off at a station on Golda Meir Boulevard, which was empty at that hour. He started walking until he noticed the inspectors had returned to him, asked him for the fine form, and one of them tore off the part containing the inspector's details.

According to the appeal, at this point, they offered him a deal: "Let's make an agreement, you won't complain about us and we won't complain about you." The teen says he stayed silent out of fear. He recounts that before they boarded another bus, one of them pulled out a badge and told him he was an undercover police officer.

Only two hours later, around midnight and on the advice of his lawyer, he called the police. According to him, the dispatcher directed him to submit an online complaint, but since he could not do so, he arrived at the station the next day to file a complaint and asked for the evidence to be collected before it could be deleted. As a result of the assault, he suffered jaw pain and was sent for medical examinations and x-rays.

September 16th, 2021: mandates. June 9th, 2022: Pfizer at Davos. October 15th, 2022: YouTube struck him for saying Pfizer had not tested transmission. January and February 2023: the Twitter Files, the White House asking Facebook to remove “often true content,” Fauci and Gates and the profit.

A working-class, left-coded, funny, spiritual man with 11.3 million people on X[8] and 6.6 million on YouTube,[9] inside British jurisdiction, naming the crime against informed consent. Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is an American problem. Brand was a British one. They already owned his sexual past. They had sold it. They did not need to invent his sins. They needed to compromise him with them.

Dame Caroline Dinenage was the officer in charge.

After she sets up Britain’s Censorship laws, Dinenage was promoted to Dame. That’s how you know this is political. In America, we call it failing upwards. Here’s the timeline:

January 2018 to February 2020: Minister of State at the Department of Health and Social Care. February 13th, 2020 to September 2021: Minister of State for Digital and Culture, the minister for Online Harms, with the Online Safety Bill in her hands through the whole of the medical order.[10] The Counter Disinformation Unit sat in that department. She answered Parliament for it.[11] 2022: made a Dame as the MP first responsible for that Bill.[12] May 2023: elected Chair of the Culture, Media and Sport Committee.[13] From May 17th, 2023 to May 30th, 2024 she also chaired its subcommittee on Online Harms and Disinformation.[14]

Her husband is Mark Lancaster, Baron Lancaster of Kimbolton. https://t.co/SklYy4Lwv8 states, in his own biography: “He is married to Caroline Dinenage.”[15] He has been reported as deputy commander of the 77th Brigade, the Army’s information-warfare formation, from 2018 to July 2020.[16] He held senior reserve posts through 2023. The household is health ministry, online harms, soldiers on the domestic information war, and the committee that cut Brand’s money.

On September 12th, 2023, four days before the film aired, she stood for the Online Safety Bill’s return. She called the regulator world class. She said the Bill would clear illegal content from the internet.[17] Then the film dropped. Then she wrote the platforms.

The people who made the film

The Sunday Times has now told us who they were, in their own celebration of the verdict.[18]

Rosamund Urwin, now chief news correspondent of the Sunday Times, began speaking to comedy and television sources in January 2019. Charlotte Wace of The Times later took the American years. Paul Morgan-Bentley, head of investigations, is named on the paper’s own account of the joint work. Ben Taylor, editor of the Sunday Times, stood over Urwin after the verdict. The Times says the investigation took four years and that in autumn 2022 Channel 4’s Dispatches formally began collaborating with the Sunday Times.[18] Channel 4’s own later review says development of the programme was formally commissioned in December 2019.[19] That is the same month the medical order was about to swallow the country, and the same years Brand was using the audience Channel 4 had given him to name the order and the destruction of informed consent.

The film was made by Hardcash Productions for Channel 4 Dispatches. Hardcash says so on its own site.[20] Ian Winter KC named Hardcash in written submissions. He called the programme a work of fiction. He told the judge that the anonymised women on screen were depicted by actors. He said the conduct of Channel 4, Hardcash, and the Sunday Times in publishing anonymous allegations was unlawful and criminal.[21]

Channel 4 is publicly owned. Its remit is set by Parliament. This was not a private scoop. It was a public corporation, a Times investigation begun in 2019, a production company, and a years-long build, dropped in the week the Online Safety Bill came back and the minister for the speech law wrote the platforms.

The week they spent the file

Saturday, September 16th, 2023. Channel 4 airs Russell Brand: In Plain Sight: Dispatches. Four anonymous women. Actors on screen for the anonymous parts, as Winter told the court.[24]

Sunday, September 17th. Channel 4 News, Anja Popp:

“There have been no formal reports to the police in connection with the allegations against Russell Brand, although in the last hour Scotland Yard said they would be speaking again to the Sunday Times and Channel 4 to ensure any victims of crime they had spoken to, were aware of how to report any criminal allegations to police.”[25]

Read that again. The Metropolitan Police had no formal reports. They went back to Rosamund Urwin’s paper and to Channel 4 so the people those journalists had already used could be walked into a criminal complaint.

The same day Channel 4 announced an internal investigation. It published a Metropolitan Police mailbox for complainants and invited more stories to Dispatches@Channel4.co.uk.[26]

Tuesday, September 19th. YouTube cuts his income under a “creator responsibility policy.” No charge.[27] The same day Dame Caroline writes Dr Theo Bertram at TikTok: confirm whether Brand monetises, including videos relating to the accusations. TikTok replies that he has never been in the Creator Fund.[28]

Wednesday, September 20th. She writes Linda Yaccarino at X Corp. Will X join YouTube in suspending his ability to earn money. Has Elon Musk personally intervened in any decision on his status. She quotes Musk: “Of course. They don’t like competition.”[29] She writes Chris Pavlovski at Rumble the same ask.[30] She wrote Meta the same day; Meta replied on September 29th.[31] There is still no charge.

Thursday, September 21st. Pavlovski calls the letter extremely disturbing. He says it is deeply inappropriate and dangerous that the UK Parliament would attempt to control who may speak on a platform or earn a living from doing so, and that singling out an individual and demanding his ban is even more disturbing given the absence of any connection between the allegations and his content on Rumble.[32]

Monday, September 25th. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, Met Central Specialist Crime: several allegations received following the media reports; anyone who believes they may have been a victim, no matter how long ago, should come forward.[33]

April 4th, 2025. First charges. Nineteen months. Jaswant Narwal, CPS:

“We carefully reviewed the evidence after a police investigation into allegations made following the broadcast of a Channel 4, Sunday Times and Times investigation in September 2023.”[35]

December 23rd, 2025. Lionel Idan, CPS, adds a 2009 rape and a 2009 sexual assault, two more women. Those later charges become two of the four counts the jury convicted. The nine-year rape term sits on a count that did not exist until twenty-seven months after Dinenage’s letters.[36]

November 5th, 2026. Jury: guilty of one rape and three sexual assaults; not guilty of two rapes and one attempted indecent assault. Remanded. David Roberts, CPS:

“The women did not report the offences to police at the time. ... The broadcast of a television programme about Brand in September 2023 prompted them, independently and for their own reasons, to come forward.”

“Given the time that has passed, the evidence available in this case was limited.”[37]

The prosecutors in court were Riel Karmy-Jones KC, Suki Dhadda, and Katie Bacon.[38] They told the jury a pattern story because, as the CPS then admitted in writing, the evidence was limited.

November 9th, 2026. Mr Justice Joel Bennathan. Ten years six months. Paragraph 1: the 2023 documentary and Times articles “empowered a number of women to come forward.” Paragraph 5: “I disregard the allegations in the documentary.” Paragraph 16: “I accept there is no sound evidential basis for me to conclude you pose a risk for the future.”[39]

They needed the film to create the case. They disowned the film as evidence. They locked him anyway. They found no future danger. His wife and children are in that sentence with him.

This is how a state fixes a speech problem. It does not answer the Nuremberg point on informed consent. It does not debate Gates or Pfizer or consent. It uses an old sexual file, fills a police book from a journalist’s list, cuts the man’s money from a committee chair’s desk, waits, charges, and calls the result justice.

What we can do now

The notice of appeal against conviction is due December 3rd, 2026. Against sentence, December 7th. Criminal Appeal Act 1968, section 18. Criminal Procedure Rules 39.2.[40]

We ran prejudicial publicity. Now we run state conflict of interest, abuse of process, and prosecutorial ethics violations.

The letters are not a culture-committee enquiry. They are an Online Harms instrument written by the minister for the speech law, four days after she pushed that law, against the man who was using a mass audience to name the medical order and the destruction of informed consent. Abuse of process. A state-created prosecution.

Here’s what we need:

The Met began with no formal reports and went to Urwin’s paper and to Channel 4. Demand every contact between Met officers and Sunday Times, Times, Channel 4, and Hardcash journalists and producers from the first of September 2023. Demand the September 17th instruction. Demand unused material on how each of the four convicted counts’ complainants first reached police. Demand every fee, reconstruction contract, appearance payment, and later book or newspaper deal in that chain. Winter already put the actors on the record. Get the contracts.

The CPS and the judge have both written that the broadcast created the complainants. Put Narwal’s April 4th, 2025 sentence, Roberts’s November 5th, 2026 sentence, and Bennathan paragraph 1 on one page. That page is the origin of the case, in the state’s own words.

Add Rumble’s letter and Pavlovski’s refusal. So do Dinenage’s offices, in order: Health, Online Harms, Dame for the speech law, Chair of Online Harms and Disinformation, the letters of September 19th and 20th. So does Lancaster’s marriage, on https://t.co/SklYy4Lwv8. So do Urwin, Wace, Morgan-Bentley, Hardcash, Mahon, Cheshire, Compton, Furphy, Narwal, Idan, Roberts, Karmy-Jones.

I will send the original PDFs of the X letter, the Rumble letter, and the sentencing remarks on request. They are already on the committee and judiciary sites.

Whatever you do, remember this: 

A man told the truth about a medical order imposed without informed consent, in violation of the Nuremberg Code. The British state answered with a rape trial. That is the case.

Robin Hood is back in jail.

What are we going to do about it?

Delhi Police asks IFF for records in its investigation of the takedown reports sent to X in its name. IFF has replied and is disclosing what it furnished.

On 13 November 2026, the Cyber Cell of the Delhi Police Crime Branch sent the Internet Freedom Foundation a notice under Section 94 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). It asks for IFF's records on the takedown reports that were sent to X in the name of a senior Delhi Police officer, and that sought the removal of our account and six of our posts. IFF replied on 14 November 2026 and furnished the records.

We are publishing the notice and our reply because our community should know when the police ask us for information, what was asked and what we gave. IFF welcomes the investigation and calls on the Delhi Police to make its findings public.

What has happened

Between 29 October and 3 November 2026, IFF with @SFLCin  and @geoblockedindia received two notices purportedly to be issued on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). X then forwarded to us two "Illegal Content Reports" submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime). On 6 November, at the hearing of our petition before the Delhi High Court, X said that the email from which the reports were submitted appears to be fake, and that it had complained to the Delhi Police. The Court recorded this and disposed of our petition, with liberty to return if any action is taken against our account or posts.

The notice is issued in FIR No. 268/2026, registered on 5 November 2026 at Police Station Crime Branch under Sections 336(3), 204 and 340(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000. These cover forgery for the purpose of cheating, personating a public servant, using a forged document or electronic record as genuine, and cheating by personation using a computer resource. The notice says the FIR concerns "unauthorized takedown requests sent to X" by someone impersonating a senior officer of the Crime Branch or another police authority.

It requires IFF to produce three things:

1) The complete trail of emails, with attachments and full headers, about the notices in the RSS's name and the takedown requests, from X or anyone else.
2) The posts we made on X on the subject, and the posts in which we were tagged.
3) Certified copies of the applications we filed before the Delhi High Court, and of its order.

It asks for a certificate under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), and for the original emails and files to be preserved.

What we furnished

Our reply went by email on 14 November, and we told the police that a printed set would follow by speed post. It carries an 87-page set of annexures and a signed certificate:

1) Fifteen emails, printed with their full headers and attachments. These are the four emails from the Proton Mail address that sent the two notices, our two replies, our email to the RSS at its official address, and the four emails from X, three of which enclose the two reports. The set also has four emails with, who received the same notices and wrote to us about them. That person is identified in them only by the account's handle and its own email address as we lack knowledge about them otherwise.

2) A list of the ten posts we published on the subject between 30 October and 6 November, with links, times and text. We did not compile posts by other users who tagged us. The other users' posts named in the reports are listed in the reports themselves.

3) A certificate under Section 63(4) of the BSA, with the hash values of the files.

The legal notice dated 3 November that our counsel served on the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), in the redacted form we published on 4 November.

On the High Court record, we said that certified copies can be obtained from the Registry, and that the Delhi Police has already been served with our petition and applications. We also told the police what we have said in public since 30 October. We do not know who sent the two notices and cannot say that they came from the RSS. We wrote to the RSS at its official address on 30 October and marked it on our reply of 1 November. It has not responded. We gave the records that bear on the notices and the reports. Much of this, including the notices, our replies, the reports and the legal notice, was already public.

IFF's position

IFF is the target of these reports and someone used the name of one of the most senior officers of the Delhi Police to try to have our account and posts removed. We said on 6 November that it is for the Delhi Police to investigate who made the reports and to say so publicly. An investigation has begun, and we have cooperated with it.

Section 94 of the BNSS allows a police officer to require a person, by written order, to produce documents needed for an investigation. We complied because this notice is confined to the records of an episode in which we are the affected party. The material was furnished without prejudice to our rights, including the liberty the High Court gave us. If we are asked for anything more, we will look at each request on its own terms, take legal advice and tell you what we can.
